first.rationale: The competitive-pricing threat makes memory_73 (promotional pricing) the tempting move, but its consolidated form records only acquisition and revenue lift at the top of the funnel and says nothing about retention, payback, or revenue quality of discount-acquired SMBs. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is exactly the omission that matters, so it is my first verification pull: if the original record shows durable, quality-controlled revenue, pricing becomes viable; if it shows a short-window acquisition spike, discounting into a competitor's price war likely buys low-value accounts and trains the segment to expect the floor price. My second pull is memory_86, because it is the memory my intended action rests on and its summary conflates two different things: completion rate (a metric that trivially rises when you shorten a flow) and time-to-value/adoption (the outcome that actually matters). I need to know whether the original showed downstream adoption or only a shorter funnel. Intended action is simplify_onboarding: onboarding completion is down 4% and activation is down 6%, and onboarding is plausibly upstream of both, so one intervention addresses the two observed declines and is corroborated by memory_31 and memory_91 pointing the same direction. It also carries the least downstream value risk of the candidates. Enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) and referral incentives (memory_57) address neither current decline; referrals also depend on an established-customer base and would not answer the SMB threat. Standard experiment scale with a holdout, and I will instrument beyond completion rate to first meaningful action, week-four retention, and revenue quality rather than declaring success on the funnel metric. All inherited claims here are compressed summaries whose original conditions and caveats may not hold at day 76 under new competitive conditions; I am treating them as priors, not findings, and both verification results could redirect this choice.
